newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hope seen for Hyundai Motor's stalled Vietnam plant.
newsitem.headline: Hope seen for Hyundai Motor's stalled Vietnam plant.

text.p: South Korea's Hyundai Motor Co could win approval to build a vehicle assembly plant in Vietnam if Chrysler Corp abandons the country's crowded market, a Vietnamese official said on Tuesday.
Deputy Minister for Industry Nguyen Xuan Chuan told Reuters that the U.S. car giant had until July to take up a construction licence which it was granted two years ago.
Local media have reported that Chrysler has abandoned its plans for a $192-million factory near Ho Chi Minh City, upset that Vietnam has issued too many licences to carmakers.
If Chrysler does bail out, Chuan said Hyundai would stand "a better chance" of seeing its application for a $230 million plant unblocked.
Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet has opposed Hyundai's southern Vietnam project, arguing that the 14 foreign joint ventures already licensed were enough for the time being.

However, Chuan said Hanoi was still open to further investment in the car sector and -- shrugging off worries that there were already too many players -- he predicted growth of at least 27 percent in the country's car market this year.
"Last year sales were about 23 percent higher than in 1995, so I would guess this year (they would be) at least 27 percent higher," he said.
Some 37,000 vehicles of all types were sold in Vietnam last year. Cars accounted for 35 percent of the total, which means that, on average, just 250 were sold per week.
A impoverished country with crumbling highways, Vietnam is hardly a bonanza market for the world's auto giants -- two wheels, not four, still rule the roads here.
Nevertheless, the prospect of growing incomes from reform-driven economic growth has been enough to lure many companies to put a foot in the door, even if it means a long wait for returns.
Seven ventures are already in operation, and Ford Motor Co of the United States is planning to roll out its first vehicle from a $102-million plant near Hanoi later this year.
Ford's rival, Chrysler, is less upbeat.

"Anywhere between 10,000 and 50,000 units annually split between 14 manufacturers doesn't make a very attractive picture," the official Vietnam Investment Review quoted Chrysler spokeswoman Jodi Armstrong as saying.
"They've granted assembly licences to anybody and their brother who wants to build a vehicle in Vietnam."
Chrysler has not officially declared that it is walking away from Vietnam and its country representative -- who moved to Bangkok from Hanoi last year -- was not available to comment.
Industry sources say overcrowding may become less of a problem if, as Chuan believes, the market grows to more than 100,000 units by 2005.
Their chief complaint is that the government, anxious to localise the production of components, restricts and heavily taxes imports of car kits.

The government recently lifted an effective ban on imports of complete knock-down 1 kits which had been in place since January, setting a quota of 3,000 for the year. That came as a relief to some companies, which said the ban could eventually have forced them to halt production lines and lay off workers.
